opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons. The first is that control research is unusually concrete. A lot of AI safety work, especially on the more theoretical side, can feel quite abstract when you're starting out, and it's hard to know whether you're making progress. With control, the question is very tangible: suppose the model you're working with might be misaligned and might actively try to undermine you. Can you still design a setup, with monitoring, auditing, restricted permissions, and so on, where you get useful work out of it without it being able to cause a catastrophe? You can build that setup, run a red team against it, and measure how well it holds up. That feedback loop is really valuable for someone new to the field.

The second reason is that the skills transfer well. To do good control work, you need to get comfortable running experiments with frontier models, building evaluation pipelines, thinking adversarially, and reasoning carefully about threat models. Those are basically the core skills you need across most of empirical AI safety, including evals, interpretability, and model organisms. So even if you later move into a different area, the time isn't wasted.

Third, I think it's genuinely neglected relative to how useful it could be in the near term. Control doesn't require us to solve alignment first. It asks what we can do if alignment fails or if we simply can't verify it. That's exactly the situation I expect labs to be in for the next few years: models that are very capable, being deployed internally on things like AI R&D, where we can't be confident they're aligned. Having robust control protocols in place for that period seems really important, and there's a lot of low-hanging fruit. Many of the basic questions haven't been answered yet, so a motivated newcomer can contribute something meaningful fairly quickly.

And finally, the bar to entry is relatively low. You don't need access to model weights or huge compute budgets for a lot of it. You can do meaningful control experiments with API access and a good research question. That makes it a good fit for independent researchers or people coming through programs like MATS.

I should add a caveat: I don't think control is the whole answer. It buys you time and reduces risk during a critical window, but it likely won't scale indefinitely to arbitrarily capable systems. So I see it as a very good starting point and an important part of the portfolio, not the endpoint.

r001.rationale: The candidate says basic control questions remain open, newcomers can contribute meaningfully fairly quickly, and many projects can be done with API access and a good research question.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes control as important in the near term and expects labs to need it over the next few years, but does not predict substantial demand within six to twelve months.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons, and they kind of stack on top of each other.

The first one is that control research is unusually tractable right now. A lot of alignment research has this property where you're working on a problem and you're not quite sure whether your contribution matters, because it depends on what future models look like, what the training setups will be, whether the threat model even materialises. Control sidesteps a lot of that. The framing is roughly: assume the model might be misaligned, assume it might be actively trying to undermine you, and then ask, what protocols can we build around it so that it still can't cause a catastrophe? That's a very concrete engineering question. You can write down the protocol, you can red-team it, you can measure how often the attacker gets through. You get feedback loops that are much faster than in most of safety.

The second reason is that it's robust to a lot of uncertainty. If alignment research succeeds and the models are basically trustworthy, great, control was a bit of extra insurance. If alignment research doesn't fully succeed, which I think is quite plausible on current timelines, then control is maybe the main thing standing between us and a really bad outcome. So it's one of the few bets that pays off in both worlds. I find that very appealing for someone who's just entering the field and doesn't yet have strong views on which threat models are most likely.

The third reason, and this is more about the person than the research, is that it teaches you the right mindset. When you do control work, you're forced to think adversarially. You have to constantly ask, okay, if I were the model and I wanted to get around this, what would I do? That habit transfers to basically everything else in safety. People who've done a year of control research tend to be much better at evaluations, at interpretability, at thinking about deployment decisions, because they've internalised that the model is not necessarily on your side.

And then there's a practical point, which is that the skills you need are mostly skills people already have. You need to be a decent ML engineer, you need to be able to build evals, you need to be somewhat creative about attack strategies. You don't need to have read ten years of alignment theory before you can contribute something useful. That lowers the barrier to entry a lot, and it means that within a few months you can produce work that the labs actually care about and might actually deploy.

I should say I don't think control is the whole answer. There are scenarios where the models are smart enough that no reasonable protocol holds, and we need to be honest about that. But as a starting point, as a way to get your hands dirty and build intuitions that generalise, I think it's one of the best entry points we have right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes control research as tractable, concrete work accessible with existing ML engineering and evaluation skills, and says newcomers can contribute within a few months.

r002.rationale: It says useful work may matter to labs within a few months, but does not predict substantial demand for control research in six to twelve months.

astra-6.text:
I think AI control is a particularly good starting point because it gives you a concrete problem that you can work on empirically. You ask: suppose the model is willing to undermine our safeguards, and it’s capable enough to cause serious harm. Can we nevertheless set up a system where we can use it safely?

That lets you get started without resolving every disagreement about why a model might become misaligned. You can have one model try to sneak something past a monitor, have another model try to catch it, and test whether different safeguards actually help. For example, can a coding assistant insert a subtle vulnerability without being detected? Does giving the monitor more time or selectively asking a human to review suspicious actions improve things?

For someone entering the field, that’s a useful feedback loop. You build an experiment, discover that your proposed defence fails in an unexpected way, and learn something about both the models and the difficulty of the problem.

The caveat is that success against today’s models doesn’t establish that the same setup will work against much more capable systems. You have to be explicit about what capabilities you’re assuming and what your experiments actually demonstrate. But that’s also good training: it forces you to connect an abstract safety argument to something you can test.

r001.rationale: It describes AI control as a concrete, empirical starting point and gives experiments a person entering the field can try.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about future demand for AI control research or a six-to-twelve-month timeframe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI control is a particularly good starting point because it gives you a concrete problem you can work on without first resolving a lot of disagreements about how future AI systems will behave. You ask: suppose this model is trying to undermine our safeguards. Can we still use it productively while preventing it from causing serious harm?

That leads to fairly practical experiments. You can have one model try to sneak a vulnerability into code, and test whether another model catches it. You can vary how much oversight you use, what information the monitor gets, and when you escalate to a human. Then you can measure both how useful the system remains and how often the attack succeeds.

For someone entering the field, that’s a useful feedback loop. You can build things, discover that your proposed defence fails, understand why, and improve it. And you learn skills that are relevant to other parts of AI safety: evaluating models, designing adversarial tests, and thinking carefully about what your evidence actually establishes.

I wouldn’t take success in those experiments as proof that we can control much more capable systems. That gap is a real research problem. But it’s a tractable place to start making progress on a question we may need to answer even if alignment turns out to be difficult.

r001.rationale: The response describes concrete, practical experiments and says they provide a useful feedback loop for someone entering the field, clearly presenting accessible projects for newcomers.

r002.rationale: The response makes no prediction about demand for AI control research over the next six to twelve months.
